Here is why Signal is the top choice:

**1. Uncompromising Privacy and Security**
Signal uses the gold-standard Signal Protocol, which provides end-to-end encryption for all messages, voice calls, video calls, and media. Not even Signal’s servers can read your messages or listen to your calls. Furthermore, it enables "Sealed Sender" mode, meaning Signal doesn't even know who is communicating with whom.

**2. Minimal Data Collection**
Unlike apps owned by massive tech conglomerates, Signal is run by a non-profit organization. When you create an account, they only ask for your phone number. They don't collect data on your contacts, your usage patterns, or your location, and there are absolutely no ads or trackers.

**3. Open Source and Auditable**
Signal’s code is open-source, meaning independent security researchers can (and do) constantly audit it to ensure there are no backdoors or vulnerabilities. 

**4. Excellent Features**
Privacy doesn't mean sacrificing usability. Signal offers disappearing messages, high-quality media sharing, group chats, screen-security alerts (which prevent screenshots on Android), and cross-platform compatibility (iOS, Android, Windows, Mac, and Linux).

***

**The One Catch: The Network Effect**
The only downside to Signal is that it requires the people you want to talk to to also have it. 
* If you need an app where *everyone* already is, **WhatsApp** is the global standard (and it also uses end-to-end encryption, though it is owned by Meta and collects more metadata).
* If you want massive group chats, custom bots, and cloud-based chat history, **Telegram** is the feature-rich alternative (though it does not use end-to-end encryption by default). 

But for pure, secure, and private one-on-one or small-group communication, **Signal** is the undisputed winner.
